old_title: Burnham open to 'honest discussion' on EU free movement
new_title: Burnham open to 'honest discussion' on EU free movement
old_text:
- Published
The prime minister says he would welcome an "honest discussion" about the prospect of returning to free movement between the UK and European Union.
Speaking to the Sunday Times, Andy Burnham said he wants to pursue a new type of relationship with Brussels, potentially including full EU membership or joining the single market, which would require free movement.
"I think you have to have a very factual, quite evidence-based debate about this," he told the newspaper.
Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said there could be "no return" to free movement after the 2016 EU referendum, while Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said the prime minister's comments were a betrayal of voters who supported Brexit.
Burnham has previously committed to Labour's 2024 election manifesto, which ruled out the return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.
He has said that any fundamental changes would require a mandate at a general election, which is due by 2029.
Migration dominated debate during the 2016 Brexit campaign, with the "leave" campaign raising issues about rules allowing any EU citizen to move to the UK.
But the prime minister suggested the type of migration experienced during the years of EU membership was "different" from the challenges faced now.
"It was generally younger people, not always, but spending a few years, then going back," he said in his told the Sunday Times., external
"And obviously the ease of that worked for British people as well."
He acknowledged that freedom of movement "had very significant challenges associated with it".
"Revolving door migration where people would come and then go back is different," he said.
"The balance of migration has changed, hasn't it, since then? I think we've just got to have an honest discussion about those things."
Burnham's willingness to re-open some of the most sensitive debates in British politics has been a feature of his first months in power.
In an interview with the BBC in September, Burnham said Britain could go "all the way" towards rejoining the European Union.
However, in his latest remarks, the prime minister stressed: "I can't see myself ever recommending anything that would involve joining the euro or Schengen."
The Schengen Agreement allows passport-free travel across EU countries. While the UK did not previously abandon the pound while it was an EU member, the bloc has pushed new members to adopt the single currency.
The remarks were made ahead of his meeting with EU chiefs at a summit on 20 November in Brussels, where he is expected to pitch options for a reset of relations with the bloc.
The shadow home secretary said EU free movement would amount to "handing back control of our borders and allowing uncontrolled migration from across Europe".
Philp said: "The British people voted to end free movement, and there can be no return to it."
Burnham won the Greater Manchester seat of Makerfield at a by-election in June, ahead of him becoming prime minister the following month. The constituency voted to leave the European Union in 2016.
As a candidate in the by-election, Burnham had promised not to "re-run" Brexit arguments and said he was "not proposing that the UK considers rejoining the EU".
In response to the Sunday Times interview, Farage said: "This is a total betrayal of Brexit Britain and his Makerfield pitch".
"He is also deluded to say immigration was different when we were members of the EU. We will fight this dishonesty," the Reform UK leader added.
new_text:
- Published
The prime minister says he would welcome an "honest discussion" about the prospect of returning to free movement between the UK and European Union.
Speaking to the Sunday Times, Andy Burnham said a new relationship with Brussels could include full EU membership or joining the single market, requiring free movement.
Migration dominated debate during the 2016 Brexit campaign, with the Leave campaign raising issues about rules allowing any EU citizen to move to the UK.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch responded the prime minister "hasn't thought this through", while Reform UK's Robert Jenrick dismissed the idea as "mad".
Burnham has previously committed to Labour's 2024 election manifesto which ruled out a return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.
He has said that any changes would require a mandate at a general election, which is due by 2029.
"I think you have to have a very factual, quite evidence-based debate about this," he told the Sunday Times, external, adding he believed the type of migration had changed from revolving door movement of young people who would return home after a few years.
"Revolving door migration where people would come and then go back is different," he said. "The balance of migration has changed, hasn't it, since then? I think we've just got to have an honest discussion about those things."
But he stressed: "I can't see myself ever recommending anything that would involve joining the euro or Schengen."
The Schengen Agreement allows passport-free travel across EU countries. The UK was able to keep the pound when it was an EU member, but the bloc has pushed new members to adopt the Euro.
His remarks were made ahead of an EU summit on 20 November in Brussels, where the prime minister is expected to pitch options for a reset of relations with the bloc.
In an interview on ITV's Good Morning Britain on Monday, Burnham said: "We have a situation now where longer term, permanent migration has replaced what was freedom of movement."
He continued: "Why has this problem arisen? Its arisen because, if you look back to the early 2020s, people call it the Boris Wave, a huge number of people came in seeking permanent settlement on longer term visas.
"That was the change I was pointing to in relation to freedom of movement and revolving door migration - a new problem has arisen for Britain in terms of how do we handle that form of migration in the long run."
He backed home secretary Shabana Mahmood's plan to increase the waiting period for indefinite leave to remain to be increased from five to up to 15 years, saying "settlement is a right to be earned, not just granted automatically".
And he said Brexit had damaged the UK's ability to control its borders, so he wanted to re-establish cooperation around immigration at next month's EU summit.
"I don't think things have worked out as people said they would at the time, particularly when it comes to immigration," he said.
"I think we've got weaker control now. The reason the small boats crisis has arisen is because we can't return people and people know we can't do that in the same way that we used to be able to do."
On the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Rayner said she wanted to see the best possible deal with the European Union, which may well involve concessions, as Burnham seeks to reset of relations with the bloc.
"What the prime minister is saying now, and what I want, is that we have an honest conversation about the facts of what the trade-offs are to get the best deal for Britain going forward," she said.
"The frustration for me in the previous debate we had when we had the referendum is that a lot of those facts didn't get the airtime... So I would like us to have an honest conversation about what the trade-offs could be and then put that to the people at a general election."
Writing on X, Badenoch dismissed it as "yet another example of Burnham's foot in mouth syndrome".
She added: "Most people who voted for Brexit did so because they didn't want free movement. Too many politicians have failed to understand the significance and impact of immigration on communities."
Conservative MP and former chancellor Jeremy Hunt, who backed Remain, warned the Brexit debate was "incredibly divisive" and insisted the current Brexit deal can still be made to work.
"I was at the top of a government that was paralysed for several years while we were trying to wrestle with the implications of that vote and I think, having made the decision, we should stick with it and make the most of it - I think we can make it a success," he told Kuenssberg.
Pointing to the one million young people not in work or training, he added: "Surely our priority in that situation is to get those jobs filled by the young people we have here instead of parking them on welfare.
"Which is why I think it's astonishing to lead on the issue of free movement... Something that is actually going to stop young people here getting jobs."
But Liberal Democrat deputy leader Daisy Cooper told Kuenssberg she believed allowing freedom of movement would be "a really good thing for growth" and pushed for the UK to rejoin the single market, the customs union, and also be involved in the bloc's defence pact.
The UK currently has "the worst of both worlds" on immigration, she said, as it was excluded from the EU's "new asylum pact with biometric data" that could be used to "tackle the small boats crisis".
Reform UK's economy spokesperson Robert Jenrick told Kuenssberg he had never believed freedom of movement "was a good thing", despite supporting the Remain position before the 2016 referendum when he was a Conservative MP.
"I think it's completely mad, the idea that this country needs more immigration," he said, claiming data shows mass migration "has been a disaster for working people, for Brits".
"The last thing they want is their wages being undercut by a load of low wage, low-skilled migrants from overseas," he added.
